1.
Introduction

The project uses the Retail Store Sales: Dirty for Data Cleaning dataset, which
consists of 12,575 transactions and 11 variables related to customers, products,
categories,
prices,
quantities,
total
spending,
payment
methods,
locations,
transaction dates,
and discount application. The dataset was designed to contain
data quality issues, providing an opportunity to develop a systematic process for
data auditing, cleaning, and imputation.

Data
processing
was
divided
into
two
stages.
First,
a
data
quality
audit
and
deterministic cleaning based on business rules were performed using Python.
Subsequently, R was used to assess missing values that could not be recovered
exactly and determine whi
ch could be addressed through statistical imputation
methods.

The
methodological
approach
focused
on
preserving
the
original
data
and
modifying values only when a validated deterministic rule or sufficient statistical
evidence supported the imputation.

Preparation for Quantity Imputation

To impute missing values in the Quantity variable, five predictors were selected:
Item,
Payment
Method,
Location,
year,
and
month.
These
variables
provide
information about the purchased product, payment method, purchase channel,
and temporal characteristi
cs of the transactions. The completeness assessment
confirmed that all five predictors were fully observed, with no missing values. This
allowed
them
to
be
included
in
the
imputation
procedure
without
requiring
additional
missing
data
treatment.
However,
t
heir
completeness
does
not
guarantee
predictive
performance,
making
it
necessary
to
assess
their
relationships with Quantity and the suitability of the selected statistical method.

14.
Construction of the Validation Sample

To evaluate imputation methods for the Quantity variable, a validation sample
was constructed by artificially masking originally observed values. Of the 11,971
records
with
available
information,
1,197
observations,
representing
approximately
10%,
were
sel
ected
and
temporarily
masked
to
assess
each
method's ability to recover known values. These cases were combined with the
604 originally missing values, resulting in a total of 1,801 records with missing
information
during
the
validation
procedure.
This
approach
allowed
imputed
quantities to be compared with the actual values of the masked observations,
providing
a
basis
for
measuring
imputation
error
and
selecting
the
best
-
performing method according to the established evaluation criteria. However, the
applicability of these results to genuinely missing observations depends on how
representative the validation sample is of re
cords with missing information.

Figure 11.
Validation Design for the Imputation of the Quantity Variable.

Source.
Prepared by the author.

Figure 1
1
shows the design used to validate the imputation methods applied to
the Quantity variable. Since it is not possible to calculate the error directly on the
604 truly missing records, because their actual values are unknown, a validation
strategy based on t
he temporary masking of observed data was used. In total,
the dataset contained 11,971 records with known Quantity values, of which 1,197
cases (10%) were artificially masked. Each imputation method then attempted to
reconstruct those values, and because t
he original values were known, it was
possible to compare the estimates with the real data and objectively measure the
imputation error. During this procedure, the 1,197 masked cases were added to
the 604 truly missing values, resulting in a total of 1,801
records without Quantity
information.
This
validation
design
made
it
possible
to
identify
the
best
-
performing imputation method before applying it to the genuinely missing cases.

15.
Comparison of Imputation Methods for Quantity

To select an imputation method for the Quantity variable, three alternatives were
evaluated:
Predictive
Mean
Matching
(PMM),
Classification
and
Regression
Trees
(CART),
and
Random
Forest.
The
comparison
was
conducted
using
artificially masked values during
validation and considering accuracy, prediction
error, and bias metrics.

PMM achieved an exact
-
match accuracy of 9.52%, which increased to 29.8%
when allowing deviations of up to one unit and to 47.5% with a tolerance of two
units. It also produced a mean absolute error (MAE) of 3.20, a root mean squared
error
(RMSE)
of
3.98,
a
nd
a
bias
of
-
0.016.
CART
achieved
an
exact
-
match

accuracy of 10.1%, slightly higher than PMM, representing a difference of 0.58
percentage
points.
Although
PMM
showed
more
favorable
results
on
the
remaining evaluation criteria, the available figures do not allow these differences
to be quantified relativ
e to CART and Random Forest. Overall, the results indicate
limited ability to recover the exact original quantities, although the near
-
zero bias
suggests
a
small
average
signed
deviation.
This
does
not
necessarily
imply
greater accuracy for individual pred
ictions; therefore, method selection should
consider error metrics alongside the distributional characteristics of the imputed
values.

17. Reconstruction of Total Spent

After
completing
the
imputation
of
Quantity
using
Predictive
Mean
Matching
(PMM),
the
missing
values
in
Total
Spent
were
reconstructed
using
the
mathematical relationship between unit price and quantity purchased:

Total Spent
=
Price Per Unit
×
Quantity

This procedure calculated all 604 missing values in Total Spent, reducing the
number of missing entries from 604 to zero and achieving 100% completeness.
No additional statistical method was required for this variable, as the transaction
amounts were calcu
lated directly from Price Per Unit and the imputed Quantity
values. However, although the reconstruction is deterministic, the results depend
on
quantities
previously
estimated
using
PMM
and
therefore
retain
the
uncertainty associated with that imputation.
Consequently, complete recovery of
Total
Spent
ensures
consistency
with
the
applied
formula
but
does
not
necessarily guarantee the accuracy of the reconstructed amounts relative to the
unknown original values.

Prepared by the author.

4
shows the treatment applied to the Total Spent variable after the imputation
of Quantity. Initially, this variable contained 604 missing values. Once the Quantity
values
were
obtained,
it
was
possible
to
reconstruct
all
604
missing
Total
Spent

records
using
the
mathematical
relationship
between
unit
price
and
quantity
purchased, so no missing values remained at the end of the process.

This result indicates that it was not necessary to build an additional statistical model
for Total Spent. Instead, total spending was calculated directly by multiplying Price
Per Unit by Quantity, allowing the use of a verifiable business rule and avoiding
a
second statistical imputation for a variable that depends on another already treated.

However, it should be noted that the reconstructed Total Spent values depend on
the
previously
imputed
values
of
Quantity.
Therefore,
although
the
mathematical
operation
used
for
reconstruction
is
exact,
the
final
result
indirectly
retains
the
uncertainty associated with the imputation of Quantity.

18.
Evaluation of Discount Applied

The Discount Applied variable contained 4,199 missing values, representing 33.39%
of the transactions in the original dataset. To assess whether these values could be
imputed, three supervised classification models were compared: logistic regression,
Class
ification
and
Regression
Trees
(CART),
and
Random
Forest.
Model
performance was evaluated using overall accuracy and balanced accuracy, with a
naive classifier achieving 50.36% accuracy as the reference.

The
results
showed
that
CART
achieved
the
highest
performance
among
the
evaluated models, with an accuracy of 50.4% and a balanced accuracy of 50.4%.
Logistic regression achieved 49.5% accuracy and 49.6% balanced accuracy, while
Random Forest recorded 48.1
% on both metrics. Although CART performed slightly
better, its improvement over the baseline classifier was only 0.04 percentage points.
This
indicates
that
none
of
the
models
achieved
a
meaningful
improvement
in
predictive performance compared with
the reference.

Consequently,
the
results
do
not
provide
sufficient
evidence
to
justify
imputing
Discount Applied using the evaluated models. Assigning values based on predictions
with this level of performance could introduce classification errors and distort the
origina
l variable distribution. Therefore, retaining the missing values, documenting
their presence, and avoiding imputations without sufficient predictive support is the
more methodologically appropriate approach.

49.5%
and
Random

However,

e
xceeded

n

hout adequate predictive support.

19.
Creation of Discount_Status

Given the limited predictive performance of the models evaluated for Discount
Applied, the decision was made to retain the missing values and create a new
variable
named
Discount_Status,
with
three
categories:
TRUE,
FALSE,
and
UNKNOWN.
This
classification
distinguishes
transactions
with
discounts,
transactions without discounts, and those for which insufficient information was
available to determine their status. The results show that 4,219 records (33.55%)
were
classified
as
TRUE,
4,157
(33.06%) as
FALSE,
and
4,199
(33.39%) as
UNKNOWN,
accounting
for
all
12,575
transactions.
The
distribution
shows
similar proportions across the three categories, although UNKNOWN represents
unobserved information rather than a third
actual discount status. This approach
preserved
the
uncertainty
associated
with
the
original
records,
avoided
imputations without sufficient predictive support, and enabled missing information
to be handled explicitly in subsequent analyses.

Prepared by the author.

Figure 1
6
shows the distribution of the Discount_Status variable, created to explicitly
preserve
both
observed
and
missing
information
regarding
discount
application.
The
results indicate that 4,219 records (33.55%) were classified as TRUE, 4,157 (33.06%)
as FALSE,
and 4,199 (33.39%) as UNKNOWN. The three categories are very similar in
size, each representing approximately one third of the 12,575 transactions.

It is important to note that the UNKNOWN category does not mean that no discount was
applied.
Its
meaning
is
different:
it
indicates
that
there
is
insufficient
information
to

determine whether a discount was applied or not. In this way, the variable distinguishes
between
known
observations
and
observations
for
which
information
is
unavailable,
avoiding unsupported imputations and explicitly preserving the uncertainty present in
the
original data.

23.
Conclusions

The data auditing, cleaning, and imputation process applied to the Retail Store
Sales:
Dirty
for
Data
Cleaning
dataset
improved
data
completeness
while
preserving all 12,575 original transactions, without deleting any records during
processing. The methodo
logy combined business rules implemented in Python
with statistical procedures developed in R, prioritizing deterministic recovery and
reserving imputation for values that could not be reconstructed exactly.

Deterministic cleaning recovered all 1,213 missing values in Item and 609 in Price
Per
Unit,
resulting
in
1,822
recoveries.
These
findings
show
that
verified
relationships
between
variables
can
be
used
to
address
data
completeness
issues without relying on
statistical estimation. However, the validity of recovered
values depends on the applicability of the business rules and the consistency of
the information used.

For the 604 missing values in Quantity, PMM, CART, and Random Forest were
compared through a validation procedure based on artificially masking known
observations. PMM showed the most favorable overall performance according to
the evaluated criteria, with
a mean absolute error (MAE) of 3.20 units, a root
mean
squared
error
(RMSE)
of
3.98,
and
a
bias
of
−0.016.
Additionally,
the

imputed distribution exhibited characteristics similar to
the observed distribution,
with means of 5.64 and 5.66, respectively. Although these results supported the
selection of PMM, individual imputation accuracy remained limited, indicating that
estimated values should be interpreted in light of the uncertaint
y associated with
the procedure.

After imputing Quantity, the 604 missing values in Total Spent were reconstructed
using the mathematical relationship between unit price and quantity purchased.
This decision avoided applying a second statistical model to a variable directly
related
to
ano
ther
that
had
already
been
estimated.
Nevertheless,
the
reconstructed amounts retain the uncertainty associated with the imputation of
Quantity, even though the calculations are mathematically consistent.

The evaluation of Discount Applied showed that the classification models had
limited predictive ability, with accuracy ranging from 48.1% to 50.4%, close to the
50.36% achieved by the baseline classifier. Given the lack of sufficient predictive
improvement
, the decision was made not to impute the 4,199 missing values in
this
variable.
Instead,
Discount_Status
was
created,
incorporating
the
UNKNOWN
category
to
identify
records
whose
discount
status
remains
unknown.
This
decision
avoided
introducing
artificial
classifications
without
adequate empirical support.

As a result, two final datasets were generated: a scientific dataset containing 14
variables, which explicitly preserves missing values in Discount Applied, and an
operational dataset containing 13 variables, with no null values but with unknown
informatio
n
identified
through
Discount_Status
.
Both
retain
all
12,575
original
transactions
and
support
different
research
and
operational
analysis
requirements.

In
conclusion,
the
main
methodological
outcome
of
the
project
was
the
development of a procedure that distinguishes originally observed values, values
recovered
through
deterministic
rules,
statistically
estimated
values,
and
information
that
remains
unkno
wn.
This distinction
supports documentation
of
data
provenance,
recognition
of
imputation
limitations,
and
prevention
of
the
assumption
that
greater
completeness
necessarily
implies
greater
accuracy.
Therefore,
the
quality
of
the
final
datasets
depends
bot
h
on
the
information
recovered
and
on
the
transparency
with
which
estimates
and
remaining
uncertainty are documented.
